paper_title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

Introduction Videos provide abundant observations of how the world changes, but rarely reveal the actions that cause those changes [13]. This missing supervision limits our ability to learn controllable world models [411] and embodied agents [1216] from internet-scale video. Latent action learning [2, 17, 18] offers way to recover such supervision directly from visual transitions. latent action model typically consists of an inverse dynamics model (IDM), which infers latent action from an observed transition, and forward dynamics model (FDM), which predicts its consequence: 𝑧𝑡 = IDM(𝑥𝑡, 𝑥𝑡+1), ^𝑥𝑡+1 = FDM(𝑥𝑡, 𝑧𝑡). Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning Figure 2 Paradigms for self-supervised latent-action learning. Existing methods learn latent actions (a) from scratch [3, 19, 20], (b) on frozen visual features [21, 22], (c) with pretrained video generator as the FDM only [23, 24], or (d) with an external video prior as auxiliary supervision [25]. Ours repurposes one pretrained video DiT as both the IDM and the FDM. compact bottleneck limits what 𝑧𝑡 can encode, encouraging it to retain important information to explain visual changes. Learning useful latent actions therefore depends on both dynamics: the IDM must infer the transition, while the FDM must depend on the inferred action to predict its consequence. Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter this pipeline  (Fig. 2)  , leaving gap on each side. On the inverse side, IDMs are learned from scratch, either on raw pixels [3, 19, 20] or on top of frozen pretrained features [21, 22, 26]. They must learn to infer actions from transitions largely through the FDMs reconstruction supervision, and such specialized latent action models are outperformed by general visual foundation models [26]. Olaf-World [25] aligns latent actions with an external video representation to improve transferability, but its IDM is still learned from scratch. On the forward side, recent methods adopt pretrained video generator as the FDM [23, 24], whose initial-frame conditioning supplies appearance, reducing its leakage into the latent actions. However, they keep the standard diffusion recipe, under which the generator can learn to disregard the latent action [24], underusing its prior as learning signal. Yet modern video Diffusion Transformers (video DiTs) [27] are pretrained at scale to model how visual states evolve over time [2834]. Their representations encode rich temporal structure, while their generative dynamics learn to predict complex visual changes. Much of the prior needed for latent action learning therefore already exists inside pretrained video generator. This raises simple question: can pretrained video DiT serve both inverse and forward dynamics for latent action learning? Doing so is nontrivial: the two dynamics place different demands on the same video prior, requiring careful control over what each can access. We introduce O2LaF, self-supervised latent-action framework built on simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize the IDM and FDM from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them independently for their respective roles. For inverse dynamics, we repurpose the video DiT as feed-forward transition encoder, where action queries extract one compact latent action per visual transition under causal temporal attention. For forward dynamics, we retain the generative role of the video DiT and introduce causal joint prediction, which predicts the future state sequence jointly, conditioned on the inferred latent actions, while preserving temporal causality. Unlike visual synthesis, where training often emphasizes intermediate-noise timesteps [35, 36], the FDM here also provides the learning signal that shapes the latent-action space. At these partially noisy timesteps, the noisy future still reveals much of the target, allowing the FDM to predict the future with little reliance on the latent action. We therefore train at high noise, which suppresses this target leakage and forces the FDM to depend on the inferred action. The two dynamics are optimized end-to-end through compact continuous latent-action space. We further systematically study how the two dynamics shape the learned action space. For example, causal joint prediction outperforms autoregressive prediction by removing clean-history shortcuts, while role-specific noise levels reveal distinct information requirements for the two dynamics. Beyond generative video priors, we also extend the repurposing principle to self-supervised predictive representation models [37] and languagesupervised video multimodal models [38] as alternative IDM backbones. Interestingly, stronger action probing performance does not necessarily translate into better downstream generative control, highlighting the importance of validating latent actions beyond probing through downstream applications. We evaluate O2LaF across camera navigation and robotic manipulation. It sets new state of the art in few-shot action probing across both discrete and continuous action spaces, indicating stronger alignment with ground-truth actions. Beyond probing, the learned actions also transfer without target adaptation, enabling 2 Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning zero-shot control across firstand third-person navigation and human-to-robot transfer in manipulation. The causal FDM readily serves as video world model, while its learned action-conditioned dynamics provide strong initialization for higher-fidelity two-stage deployment. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce O2LaF, self-supervised latent-action framework that repurposes pretrained video DiT into end-to-end trained inverse and forward dynamics models. Through systematic study, we show that latent-action learning depends critically on how the two dynamics are factorized and what information they receive. O2LaF achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing across camera navigation and robotic manipulation, while demonstrating strong zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments and reusable action-conditioned dynamics for world modeling. 2. Related Work 2.1. Latent Action Learning from Videos Latent action learning turns large-scale action-unlabeled video into reusable intermediate control representation. The same representation can be consumed by world model to control future visual evolution [3, 20, 22, 25, 39], or produced by policy or planner as surrogate for physical actions [2, 19, 21, 4042]. Recent work further seeks to make this control space transferable across contexts and embodiments [25, 4345]. Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter the inverseforward dynamics pipeline  (Fig. 2)  . Early approaches learn both transition inference and prediction directly from the target videos [2, 3, 19, 20]. To reduce shortcuts from raw-pixel reconstruction, later methods move the prediction target into pretrained semantic feature spaces, emphasizing motion and task-relevant change over appearance details [21, 41, 46]. related direction strengthens the forward model with pretrained video priors, reducing appearance burden or replacing the from-scratch FDM [23, 24, 47]. Pretrained video representations have also been used as external temporal supervision to orient latent actions across visual contexts [25]. Orthogonal to where the prior enters, prior work also constrains the latent space through discrete or continuous bottlenecks [22, 47, 48], semantic or cross-view objectives [4952], motion and consistency supervision [5356], and physical or geometric grounding [40, 57]. These constraints are complementary to the structural question of how the dynamics themselves are initialized. Motivated by the shared need for transition reasoning in both inverse and forward dynamics, O2LaF repurposes the same pretrained video DiT for both. 2.2. Repurposing Pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers Pretrained video generative models encode reusable spatiotemporal structure beyond synthesis. Prior work exploits their internal representations for correspondence, tracking, and geometry [5860], while more recent methods repurpose the generative backbone itself for feed-forward perception and temporal reasoning [6163]. Together, these works show that video generative pretraining provides reusable temporal computation, not only synthesis model. This repurposing is increasingly extending to action learning. Recent robot-policy and world-action models use pretrained video generators as predictive representations, policy backbones, or priors for action experts [6469]. These methods transfer video priors into learning physical action space grounded by robot supervision. O2LaF instead uses the video prior to discover the action representation itself from action-free video. 3. Method We introduce O2LaF, self-supervised latent action learning framework. Our key premise is that large-scale video pretraining already captures how visual states evolve, which both inverse and forward dynamics need. We therefore initialize both from the same pretrained prior, but adapt each to its role by controlling what information it can access. 3 Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning Figure 3 Action-aware response in pretrained video DiT. First, do the learned latent actions align with real controls across discrete navigation and continuous manipulation (Sec. 4.2)? Second, can the same actions serve as unified control interface for video world model in unseen visual contexts, without target-specific adaptation (Sec. 4.3)? 4.1. Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate O2LaF across two domains with distinct visual dynamics. For camera navigation, we train on MiraData [75] and evaluate on MIND [76]. For robot manipulation, we train exclusively on egocentric human demonstrations from EgoDex [77] and directly evaluate on in-lab GR-1 robot demonstrations [39]. MiraData captures global scene and camera motion, whereas EgoDex focuses on fine-grained handobject interactions. No action annotations are used to train the latent action models. Baselines. We compare with representative latent-action methods spanning the learning paradigms illustrated in Fig. 2. For navigation, we compare with AdaWorld [20] and Olaf-World [25], all trained on the same MiraData videos. For manipulation, we compare with DreamDojo [39], VideoWorld2 [23], LAPA-DINOv3 [19, 26], and VILLA-X [40] using their released models. Notably, O2LaF uses only EgoDex subset of DreamDojos large scale egocentric training data. We evaluate representation quality using frozen encoders under identical probing protocols, and action-conditioned generation through controlled second-stage world-model comparison. Implementation details. Both the IDM and FDM of O2LaF are initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and adapted with rank-128 LoRA. The IDM uses causal video-token attention, while the FDM uses frame-causal attention with joint future prediction. We use 32-D Gaussian latent action with 𝛽 = 104 and keep the video VAE and text encoder frozen. We therefore freeze each latent-action encoder and fit lightweight linear probes [78] across increasing label budgets to evaluate control decodability. Evaluation protocol. We evaluate discrete camera control and continuous robot manipulation. On MIND, we predict four simultaneous ternary controls (two translation and two rotation axes) using independent, class-balanced logistic regression probes. We report joint exact-match accuracy, requiring all four predictions to be correct. For manipulation, we use DreamDojos In-lab Eval benchmark [39], comprising GR-1 robot demonstrations. We fit Ridge regression probes for wrist translation and rotation on both arms. We report EEF 𝑅2, averaged over translation, rotation, and both arms. Label budgets range from 1 to 50 videos for navigation and 1 to 32 episodes per task for manipulation. Results. Fig. 6 shows that O2LaF consistently improves linear decodability across domains and label budgets. Performance rises sharply with the first few labeled examples, indicating that control-relevant information is readily accessible with limited supervision. Notably, O2LaF achieves an EEF 𝑅2 of 0.277 on GR-1, compared with 0.149 for DreamDojo, despite training its encoder exclusively on human demonstrations without robotdomain adaptation, suggesting that the learned latent actions capture motion structure transferable across human and robot embodiments. Understanding the Two Dynamics Although sharing the same pretrained video prior, the IDM and FDM serve distinct roles in latent action learning. We systematically investigate how their design choices shape the learned action representations and their utility for controllable video generation. 5.1. Adapting Pretrained Dynamics Pretrained video DiTs encode rich spatiotemporal knowledge, but their representations are not explicitly optimized for action inference. We investigate whether this knowledge can be extracted through lightweight action head or requires adapting the pretrained backbone. Since the IDM learns through predictive supervision from the FDM, we further study whether stronger FDM improves the learned action representations. Tab. 3a shows that frozen video DiT with trainable action head performs substantially worse than LoRA adaptation, while rank-16 LoRA approaches rank-128 performance. Meanwhile, scaling the FDM from 1.3B to 14B consistently improves action decodability with fixed-size IDM (Tab. 3b). These results suggest that effective latent-action learning benefits from both adapting pretrained representations and strengthening predictive supervision. 5.2. Controlling Information Exposure We revisit how the information-access designs of our two dynamics shape latent-action learning. Temporal factorization. It highlights that action probing alone does not reveal whether latent actions also encode task-irrelevant information that may hinder transfer. Downstream generative evaluation is therefore essential for assessing the transferability of learned action representations. 5.4. Balancing Action Learning and Generation Jointly learning latent actions and generative video world model is compelling objective [24]. Yet the FDM faces practical trade-off: learning informative actions requires limiting visual shortcuts, whereas high-fidelity generation benefits from broader noise coverage. In O2LaF, causal prediction and high-noise supervision serve the former objective, but compromise the latter. We investigate whether both objectives can be reconciled within end-to-end training. We first study FDM noise sampling and IDM gradient routing. Tab. 5 shows that mixed noise sampling substantially improves generation over high-noise-only training while maintaining comparable action probing performance. However, restricting IDM gradients to high-noise timesteps provides no consistent probing gains. Moreover, initializing from the jointly trained FDM, rather than the original pretrained video DiT, further improves both visual quality and action-following fidelity. 6. Conclusion We presented O2LaF, self-supervised framework that repurposes pretrained video DiT for both inverse and forward dynamics. By tailoring the two dynamics to their distinct roles and controlling information access, O2LaF learns transferable latent actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, it achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and enables zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and humanrobot embodiments. These findings establish pretrained video generators as reusable dynamics priors for action discovery and controllable world modeling. Limitations and future work. sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: The document provides supplementary information not elaborated on in our main paper due to space constraints: implementation details (Section A), visualization of action-query attention (Section B.1) and analysis of training data composition (Section B.2), two applications that use the IDM as motion annotator and the FDM as policy verifier (Section C), and discussion of limitations and future directions (Section D). A. Implementation Details A.1. End-to-End Latent-Action Learning Both the IDM and FDM are initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [70], with frozen video VAE and text encoder. We adapt both video DiTs using rank-128 LoRA, while directly training the IDM action queries and Gaussian readout, and the FDM action embedder. Each visual transition is represented by 32-dimensional Gaussian latent action. The IDM uses frame-causal attention with pairwise action queries, while the FDM uses frame-causal attention to denoise future frames conditioned on clean initial frame. Training configurations are summarized in Tab. 6. A.2. Two-Stage Video World Model To improve visual generation quality, we freeze the learned IDM as latent-action extractor and train separate bidirectional Wan2.2-TI2V-5B world model conditioned on the extracted actions. The FDM is fully fine-tuned at 832 480 resolution. By default, the FDM is initialized from the pretrained text/image-to-video model. For the E2E-init setting, we instead initialize it from the jointly trained causal FDM, providing an initialization already aligned with the learned latent-action space. Analyzing Training Data Composition Although learned without action annotations, latent-action representations still depend on the motion and embodiment diversity of the training videos. We compare four configurations: MiraData [75] (navigation), EgoDex [77] (human manipulation), EgoDexMix (human and robot manipulation), and joint MiraData/EgoDexMix training. EgoDexMix augments human demonstrations with real robot videos from GR-1 [39] and PH2D [86]. All configurations are evaluated on MIND and In-lab GR-1 following Sec. 4.2. Notably, compared with human-only EgoDex, EgoDexMix also improves third-person navigation accuracy. Joint MiraData/EgoDexMix training largely preserves navigation performance while improving robot probing over MiraData alone. Applications C.1. IDM as Motion Annotator O2LaF learns latent actions by explaining visual transitions, without explicit motion annotations. Can self-supervised IDM provide better foundation for fine-grained motion understanding? We investigate this on CameraBench [87], which evaluates 15 camera-motion categories. We consider two backbone scales: 270M spatial-temporal Transformer trained from scratch and fully fine-tuned, and 5B video DiT initialized from Wan2.2 and adapted with rank-128 LoRA (322M trainable parameters). We compare supervised camera-motion recognition with and without latent-action pretraining, using 1,114 labeled CameraBench training clips (1.78 hours). We additionally probe frozen IDMs with lightweight MLP heads to assess their motion understanding without backbone adaptation. As shown in Tab. 8, latent-action pretraining substantially improves supervised motion recognition, yielding gains of 44.9 and 9.2 AP for the spatial-temporal Transformer and pretrained video DiT, respectively. Notably, the latter improvement comes on top of strong video generative pretraining, suggesting that inverse-dynamics learning captures motion information beyond generic video representations. Even without backbone adaptation, frozen IDM features remain highly effective for motion recognition. Together, these results establish selfsupervised inverse dynamics as promising foundation for motion annotation, with potential extensions to dense temporal labeling and feedback for controllable video generation. C.2. FDM as Policy Verifier Frontier AI models are quickly becoming capable robot agents: they write robot policies as code [88] and control two-armed robot from camera images in simulation [89]. Such agents are increasingly built and tested in simulators, but simulator only approximates the real scene, and real-robot trials are slow and costly [90], so behavior that succeeds in simulation may still fail on the robot. Our FDM offers cheap check across this gap: starting from real photo, it predicts what candidate action sequence will do in the real scene, before the robot executes it. For each scene, Opus 5.5 (high) rebuilds MuJoCo [91] simulation from the robots head-camera photo, using the GR-1 model from robosuite [92]. We then script candidate grasps and run them in physics as reference. To query the FDM, we render each trajectory with all movable objects removed, so the latent actions the IDM extracts describe the robots motion but not the simulated outcome, and roll them out from the real photo. When the two agree (Fig. 12a,b), the FDM reproduces both successful placement and failed grasp, while keeping details the rebuild simplifies, such as the real pan. When they disagree (Fig. 12c), the simulator lifts salt shaker that, in the FDM rollout, stays on the table. The rebuilt scene suggests cause: the small tapered glass shakers with metal caps become taller plain cylinders, and the glass vase beside them becomes an opaque cylinder, so grasp that fits the rebuilt shaker may miss the real one. Without executing the trajectory we cannot tell which prediction is right, but such disagreement flags an action worth checking before it reaches the robot. We see this pre-execution check as promising direction for future work. 20 Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning Figure 12 The FDM as policy verifier on GR-1 humanoid. Each case shows one trajectory in the physics simulator rebuilt from single photo (top), the same motion with objects removed, from which latent actions are extracted (middle), and the FDM rollout from the real photo (bottom). D. Limitations and Future Work O2LaF learns transferable latent actions from unlabeled videos, but several challenges remain. Structure and interpretability of latent actions. Although our learned actions transfer across visual contexts and embodiments, their underlying structure remains poorly understood. Beyond quantitative probing, interpreting individual latent actions still largely relies on inspecting their corresponding reference videos. Learning more interpretable, compositional, and appearance-invariant action representations remains an important direction for future work. Toward decision-making world models. O2LaF learns latent actions that explain visual transitions and control future video generation. However, its dynamics are optimized for visual prediction rather than decision-making. Unlike compact dynamics models that support efficient imagined rollouts and policy optimization [5, 93], video diffusion models incur substantial computational costs and do not directly expose executable actions or task-relevant rewards. Bridging video-derived action representations with efficient, decision-relevant dynamics is an important direction toward planning and closed-loop control.
